ai_root_cause: PC3 in Accounting is connected to Fa0/5, which is incorrectly assigned to VLAN 30 (Marketing), preventing it from communicating with the file server in VLAN 20 (Accounting)
expected_fault: Port Fa0/5 is assigned to VLAN 30 (Marketing) instead of VLAN 20 (Accounting), so PC3 is in the wrong broadcast domain and cannot reach VLAN 20 resources.

ai_root_cause: Native VLAN mismatch between SW1 and SW2 on the trunk link, causing intermittent drops of management VLAN frames and CDP errors
expected_fault: Native VLAN mismatch on the trunk link between SW1 (native VLAN 1) and SW2 (native VLAN 99) causes untagged frames to be mishandled and management traffic to be dropped.

ai_root_cause: VLAN 50 (Engineering) is not allowed on the trunk between SW1 and SW2, preventing PCs in VLAN 50 on SW2 from reaching the file server in VLAN 50 on SW1
expected_fault: VLAN 50 is not in the allowed VLAN list on the trunk port Gi0/1 (only VLANs 1, 10, 20 are allowed), so VLAN 50 traffic cannot cross between SW1 and SW2.

ai_root_cause: VLAN 40 is not configured on SW2, despite Fa0/10 being assigned to it, causing the port to not forward traffic and the PC to receive an APIPA address
expected_fault: VLAN 40 has not been created on SW2 (it does not appear in show vlan brief), so the port is assigned to a non-existent VLAN and all traffic is dropped.

ai_root_cause: The interface Fa0/12 on SW1 is configured as a trunk port, but it should be an access port in VLAN 10 to allow the PC to get a DHCP address and have connectivity
expected_fault: Port Fa0/12 is configured as a trunk port instead of an access port in VLAN 10. The PC cannot interpret 802.1Q-tagged frames and fails to communicate. The ACL on R1 is a red herring — it correctly permits VLAN 10 traffic.
corrected_diagnosis: VLAN 20 is not assigned to interface Fa0/2.
reviewer_notes: AI identified the issue as routing, but it was just a missing switchport access vlan command.

ai_root_cause: PC1's default gateway is incorrectly configured as 10.10.10.2 instead of the expected 10.10.10.1, which is the IP address of R1's Gi0/0.10 interface
expected_fault: PC1's default gateway is manually set to 10.10.10.2 which does not exist; the correct gateway address is 10.10.10.1 (R1's Gi0/0.10 subinterface).

ai_root_cause: The Gi0/0.10 subinterface serving VLAN 10 is administratively down, preventing PCs on VLAN 10 from reaching other VLANs or the internet
expected_fault: Router subinterface Gi0/0.10 is administratively down (shutdown), so R1 cannot serve as the gateway for VLAN 10. VLAN 20 works because Gi0/0.20 is up/up.

ai_root_cause: The subnet mask configured on the VLAN 20 gateway (R1 Gi0/0.20) is incorrect, causing PCs with IPs above 10.10.20.15 to be on a different subnet and unable to reach the gateway
expected_fault: R1's Gi0/0.20 subinterface is configured with a /28 subnet mask (255.255.255.240) instead of /24 (255.255.255.0), so only hosts in the 10.10.20.0-10.10.20.15 range are considered local; hosts above .15 are unreachable from the gateway.

ai_root_cause: The SVI for VLAN 30 has an incorrect IP address (10.10.30.2) which does not match the expected gateway IP (10.10.30.1) for PCs in VLAN 30
expected_fault: The SVI for VLAN 30 has IP address 10.10.30.2 but the PCs are configured with default gateway 10.10.30.1. No device owns 10.10.30.1 so the gateway is unreachable.

ai_root_cause: IP routing is disabled on MLS1, preventing it from routing traffic between VLANs 10 and 20
expected_fault: The 'ip routing' command has not been enabled on the L3 switch (show run confirms 'no ip routing'). Without it, the switch cannot route between VLANs even though both SVIs are up. The pruned VLAN 30 on the trunk is a red herring — it is irrelevant to the inter-VLAN routing failure.
corrected_diagnosis: Default gateway is configured correctly on the PC, but the switch SVI is down.
reviewer_notes: AI blamed the gateway IP itself, but the gateway interface is administratively down.

ai_root_cause: DHCP pool for VLAN10-POOL is exhausted, with all 30 available addresses leased, causing new devices to receive APIPA addresses and preventing existing devices from renewing their leases
expected_fault: DHCP pool for VLAN 10 is completely exhausted — all 30 addresses in the /27 scope are leased. New clients receive no offer and fall back to APIPA. The pool should be expanded to a /24 to accommodate all hosts.

ai_root_cause: The DHCP pool VLAN10-POOL is configured with the wrong subnet (10.10.20.0/24) instead of the intended VLAN 10 subnet (10.10.10.0/24), causing PCs to receive incorrect IP addresses
expected_fault: DHCP pool VLAN10-POOL is configured with the wrong network statement — 10.10.20.0/24 instead of 10.10.10.0/24. Clients receive addresses from the wrong subnet and cannot communicate on their actual VLAN.

ai_root_cause: Missing ip helper-address on MLS1's VLAN 40 SVI, preventing DHCP requests from VLAN 40 PCs from being forwarded to R1
expected_fault: The ip helper-address command is missing on MLS1's SVI Vlan40 interface. DHCP broadcast DISCOVERs from VLAN 40 clients are not relayed to the DHCP server (R1) on the remote subnet. VLAN 10 works because it is on the same subnet as R1.

ai_root_cause: DHCP excluded-address range 10.10.10.1–10.10.10.250 is overly broad, leaving only 4 usable addresses (.251–.254); the pool's 'Total addresses: 254' is misleading because the exclusion negates nearly all of them
expected_fault: The DHCP excluded-address range 10.10.10.1 through 10.10.10.250 is overly broad, leaving only 4 usable addresses (.251-.254). The pool's total of 254 addresses is a red herring — the exclusion negates nearly all of them.
corrected_diagnosis: DHCP pool is exhausted because of excluded addresses, not total size.
reviewer_notes: AI said the pool was large enough, completely missing the ip dhcp excluded-address range.

ai_root_cause: The default-router IP address configured in the DHCP pool (10.10.10.254) does not match the IP address of the gateway interface (10.10.10.1) on R1, causing PCs to use an incorrect gateway IP
expected_fault: DHCP pool default-router is set to 10.10.10.254 (no device exists at that address) instead of 10.10.10.1 (R1's actual gateway interface). PCs receive the wrong gateway via DHCP and cannot route off-subnet.

ai_root_cause: The DNS server IP address pushed by DHCP (10.10.10.50) does not match the actual DNS server IP address (10.10.10.5), causing DNS resolution failures
expected_fault: DHCP pool distributes the wrong DNS server address — 10.10.10.50 (non-existent) instead of 10.10.10.5 (the actual DNS server). Clients send DNS queries to a host that does not exist.

ai_root_cause: ACL 120 on R1's Gi0/0.10 sub-interface blocks incoming UDP DNS requests (deny udp any any eq 53), preventing PCs from resolving names despite having the correct DNS server IP
expected_fault: ACL 120 on R1 Gi0/0.10 explicitly denies UDP port 53 (line 40) before the permit-all on line 50, blocking DNS query traffic. The DHCP dns-server configuration is correct — a red herring that makes it appear the DNS setup is fine.
corrected_diagnosis: DNS server address provided via DHCP is incorrect.
reviewer_notes: AI said DNS was reachable, but the IP handed out to clients is wrong.

ai_root_cause: DHCP server is not providing DNS server information to clients, resulting in failed name resolution
expected_fault: The DHCP pool is missing the dns-server option entirely. PCs receive an IP and gateway via DHCP but no DNS server address, so all name resolution fails.

ai_root_cause: The DNS server (10.10.10.5) has an incomplete ARP entry on R1, indicating that R1 has not received an ARP response from the DNS server, likely due to the DNS server not sending ARP replies or a Layer 2 issue
expected_fault: The DNS server at 10.10.10.5 is powered off or its NIC is disconnected — ARP resolution for 10.10.10.5 shows 'Incomplete' on R1. The switch port being up/connected is a red herring (the port may be connected but the server's NIC or OS is not responding).
corrected_diagnosis: Host has no route to the external DNS server.
reviewer_notes: AI focused on DNS server availability instead of basic reachability/routing.

ai_root_cause: The static route on R1 to the server farm (10.10.30.0/24) via R2 (10.10.99.2) may be incorrect or incomplete, as PCs on VLAN 10 can reach VLAN 20 but not the server farm, and traceroute stops at R1
expected_fault: R1 has a static route to 10.10.30.0/24 via R2, but R2 has no return route to 10.10.10.0/24 or 10.10.20.0/24. Packets reach the server farm but replies are dropped by R2 because it has no route back.

ai_root_cause: Incorrect next-hop IP in the static route to 192.168.1.0/24 — the IP 10.10.99.5 does not match the IP of R2's S0/0/0 interface (10.10.99.2)
expected_fault: Static route to 192.168.1.0/24 on R1 points to next-hop 10.10.99.5, which does not exist on the serial link (the valid peer is 10.10.99.2). The link being up is confirmed but the next-hop is unreachable.

ai_root_cause: R2 is not advertising the 172.16.10.0/24 network to R1 via OSPF because it is not included in the OSPF network configuration
expected_fault: The 172.16.10.0 network is not included in R2's OSPF network statements (only 10.10.99.0 is advertised). OSPF does not advertise Gi0/1's subnet, so R1 never learns the route.

ai_root_cause: OSPF area mismatch between R1 and R2: R1 is configured for Area 0 while R2 is configured for Area 1, preventing neighbor adjacency formation
expected_fault: R1's Gi0/0 is in OSPF Area 0 while R2's Gi0/0 is in OSPF Area 1. OSPF requires matching area IDs on a shared link to form adjacency. The network statements and wildcard masks are correct — a red herring that suggests the OSPF config looks fine at first glance.
corrected_diagnosis: Missing static route for the 10.1.2.0/24 network.
reviewer_notes: AI pointed out a trunk issue, but the routing table is actually missing the route.

ai_root_cause: The static route to the data centre network (172.16.0.0/16) is configured to use the slow serial WAN path (via 10.10.99.2) instead of the direct GigabitEthernet link (via Gi0/1 to R3)
expected_fault: The static route to 172.16.0.0/16 directs traffic via 10.10.99.2 (the slow Serial WAN link to R2) instead of 10.10.50.2 (the direct GigabitEthernet link to R3). Traffic takes an unnecessary multi-hop WAN path.

ai_root_cause: ACL 101 on R1's Gi0/0.10 interface is blocking inbound TCP traffic from VLAN 10 to the web server at 10.10.30.10 on port 80, preventing HTTP browsing
expected_fault: ACL 101 line 20 explicitly denies TCP port 80 (HTTP) traffic from VLAN 10 to host 10.10.30.10. ICMP is permitted on line 10, which is why ping works. The deny rule should be removed or changed to permit.

ai_root_cause: The ACL 150 is applied as an outgoing access list on the internal interface Gi0/0.30, which prevents external traffic from reaching the web server because incoming traffic is not subject to this ACL; instead, it should be applied as an incoming access list on the external interface S0/0/0
expected_fault: ACL 150 is applied outbound on the internal Gi0/0.30 interface instead of inbound on the external S0/0/0 interface. Inbound internet traffic on S0/0/0 has no ACL (no filtering), but the permit rules on Gi0/0.30 outbound reference the internal IP which never matches post-NAT traffic flow. The ACL should be applied inbound on S0/0/0 and reference the public IP.

ai_root_cause: The ACL 130 applied to Gi0/0.20 only permits outgoing traffic from VLAN 10 (10.10.10.0/24) to any destination on ports 80, 443, and ICMP, effectively blocking all other traffic including traffic from VLAN 20 to its own gateway
expected_fault: ACL 130 only has permit statements for the 10.10.10.0/24 (VLAN 10) source network. There is no permit statement for 10.10.20.0/24 traffic. The implicit deny all at the end of the ACL drops all VLAN 20 traffic. The administrator applied a VLAN 10 ACL to the VLAN 20 interface by mistake.

ai_root_cause: ACL 140 on R1's Gi0/0.10 interface is blocking ICMP packets from VLAN 10 to VLAN 30, preventing PC1 from pinging the server at 10.10.30.5
expected_fault: ACL 140 line 10 explicitly denies all ICMP traffic from VLAN 10 to VLAN 30, blocking ping while allowing TCP (HTTP/SSH) and UDP through subsequent permit rules.

ai_root_cause: ACL 105 on R1's Gi0/0.10 interface has a rule (line 10) that only permits IP packets from the 10.10.10.0/25 subnet (10.10.10.0–10.10.10.127) to the file server at 10.10.30.5, effectively blocking hosts with IPs 10.10.10.128–10.10.10.254
expected_fault: ACL 105 line 10 uses wildcard mask 0.0.0.127 which only matches hosts 10.10.10.0 through 10.10.10.127. Hosts in the .128-.254 range do not match line 10, fall through to the deny on line 20, and are blocked. The wildcard mask should be 0.0.0.255 to cover the entire /24.

ai_root_cause: The NAT inside interface is not properly configured on Gi0/0.10, preventing internal PCs from being translated to the external IP address for internet access
expected_fault: The interfaces are not designated as NAT inside or NAT outside (ip nat inside / ip nat outside commands are missing from both interface configurations). NAT cannot function without these designations, so no translations are created.

ai_root_cause: The NAT ACL (access list 10) only permits translation for source IPs in the 10.10.10.0/24 network, excluding the 10.10.20.0/24 network from PAT, thus preventing VLAN 20 PCs from accessing the internet
expected_fault: NAT access list 10 only permits the 10.10.10.0/24 network. The 10.10.20.0/24 network is not included, so VLAN 20 traffic is never translated and is dropped at the ISP edge.

ai_root_cause: NAT pool exhaustion due to insufficient public IPs in the NATPOOL for the number of concurrent users, leading to 'destination unreachable' errors during peak hours
expected_fault: NAT pool NATPOOL contains only 4 public IP addresses (209.165.200.225-228) with non-overload (one-to-one) mapping. When all 4 are allocated, additional translations fail (312 misses). The pool should use overload (PAT) or be expanded.

Static NAT maps 203.0.113.10 to inside local address 10.10.10.50, but the actual web server's IP is 10.10.10.15. The NAT translation sends traffic to a non-existent host. The ACL correctly permits HTTP/HTTPS to the public IP — a red herring suggesting the ACL is the issue when it actually has zero matches because NAT is translating to the wrong host.
corrected_diagnosis: NAT pool exhaustion; no IP addresses left in the NAT pool.
reviewer_notes: AI timed out or failed to provide a diagnosis, but the NAT pool was clearly exhausted.
